Basic sorting algorithms
Bubble sort:
Compares consecutive items swaps them if they are in incorrect order
 Repeat until a clean pass: no more swaps are necessary
Insertion sort: 
Insert one item at a time in the right position in a partial sorted array. 
Repeat until all items are sorted
Selection sort: 
Find the smallest item and move it in the first position; 
Find the second smallest, move it in the second position
Repeat until the end of the array.

What is a ‘pass’?
A pass is a for loop that does something through each element of a list
Ex. You need one pass to find the maximum item of an array. 
What is a ‘swap’?
A swap is a switch of values in two different positions in the array.
Ex. Swap values in indices 3 and 5.

●

●

How Codebreakers Use Frequency Analysis
●
The codebreaker ﬁrst counts the 
occurrences of each letter or symbol in 
the intercepted ciphertext.
●
They then compare these observed 
frequencies with the known standard 
letter frequencies of the language 
●
They make educated guesses about the 
mappings. For example : The most 
frequent letter in ciphertext is likely ‘E’. 
The second most frequent is likely ‘T’., 
and so on.

The codebreaker looks for more 
common words, single-letter words like 
‘A’ or “i’, two letter pairs like ‘TH’, ‘ER’ 
and  trigrams  like ‘THE’, ‘AND’, ‘FOR’.

Through a process of trial and error, the

Message would be written around a tube and then unwrapped to be sent.  Message would need to be warped around an identical tube to be read.

Islamic Golden Age
Al Kindi (9th century) invented a frequency analysis to break substitution ciphers.
This was the first scientific approach to codebreaking.
This shifted cryptography form being a form of art to a type of science.
Also the age where Steganography emerged, which is the act of hiding messages in plain sight.

[Slide 5]
Renaissance
Vigenere Cipher utilized a key to vary letter shifts. (Instead of using fixed shifts like earlier ciphers.
This newer version of a shifting cipher was considered unbreakable at the time.
In this period Cryptography went over mathematical formalization.
Cryptography became political and diplomatic and was utilized in royal courts and espionage.

[Slide 6]
Mechanization
The Jefferson Disk invented by Thomas Jefferson in the 1790s was a machine that utilized rotating disks to encipher and decipher messages.
Rotor Machines were invented utilizing electrical rotors to automate substitution ciphers.
The Enigma Machine invented by Arthur Scherbius was utilized by the German military and was more complex for better encryptions.  Was later cracked by Allied efforts and was the centerpiece of WWII cryptography.

[Slide 7]
Cryptography in World War II
Both sides of the war had utilized different encryption methods in order to encrypt messages from enemies.
Lorenz Cipher was an early case of digital codebreaking utilized by the Germans.
The SIGABA and Typex were American and British encryption machines and they weren’t broken by the Axis powers.
These machines were utilized throughout the majority of the war.

[Slide 8]
Digital Revolution
The Data Encryption Standard (DES), developed by IBM and adopted by the U.S. National Bureau of Standards, utilized a 56-bit key for symmetric encryption.
This became the first federal encryption standard but was eventually deemed to insecure.
Public Key cryptography, introduced by Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman solved the problem of secure key exchange over insecure channels.
It utilized a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption.

[Slide 9]
Modern Day
Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) replaced the DES .  It uses 256-bit keys for symmetric encryption.
While AES and DES are more advanced than earlier encryption methods, they still use the same key for both encryption and decryption. (Just like earlier methods such as the Caesar cipher)
Its now the global standard for encrypting data at rest and in transit. And its used in everything from Wifi to cloud storage and VPNs.

def _chi_squared_score(text: str) -> float:
